findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GO INTERFACES: FIELD NOTES. `var e error = p` where `p` is a nil `*MyErr` — and `e != nil` is true."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the series label later: "`var e error = p` where `p` is a nil `*MyErr` — and `e != nil` is true. That one line has broken more Go services than any race condition... Part 2 of GO INTERFACES: FIELD NOTES."

findings.summary: The headline type-switch snippet does not compile because `int` appears in two cases, which is exactly the compile error the bullet underneath describes.
findings.evidence: "case int:        use(v) // v is int" followed by "case int, int64: use(v) // v stays any", with the bullet "Duplicate cases are a compile error"
findings.fix: Change the multi-type case so it does not repeat `int`, e.g. `case int32, int64: use(v) // v stays any`.

findings.summary: The page titled "Type Assertions and Type Switches" never shows the assertion syntax itself — neither the panicking single-value form nor the comma-ok form is introduced, yet comma-ok is used in the code and its result is referenced in the cost table.
findings.evidence: Page 1 opens at "Type Switch Shape" with `switch v := i.(type)`; the only assertion syntax shown is `if wt, ok := w.(io.WriterTo); ok {`, and the table row "nil interface | immediate false" refers to an `ok` value that has not been defined. The term is first named on page 5: "#9 Forgetting comma-ok turns a mismatch into a panic".
findings.fix: Add a short code block as the first block of page 1, before "Type Switch Shape": `s := i.(string)` with the panic text `interface conversion: interface {} is int, not string`, then `s, ok := i.(string)` with a note that on failure `ok` is false and `s` is the zero value — so the type switch and the `ok` column both rest on something already shown.

findings.summary: `sort.Interface` is not the widest interface in the standard library, so calling three methods the fat outlier is false.
findings.evidence: "`sort.Interface` is the fat outlier at three"
findings.fix: Reword to "`sort.Interface` at three is already on the wide side; `net.Conn` (8) and `os.FileInfo` (6) are the real outliers."

findings.summary: The func-typed adapter is offered as the mocking technique but never shown, even though the page has room for code and the mechanism (a func type with a method) is not guessable.
findings.evidence: "A one-method seam mocks with a func-typed adapter" — the only code on the page is `io.Copy(dst Writer, src Reader)` and `func Logging(n http.Handler) http.Handler`.
findings.fix: Add two lines to the payoff-patterns code block showing the pattern concretely, e.g. `type readerFunc func([]byte) (int, error)` / `func (f readerFunc) Read(b []byte) (int, error) { return f(b) }`.

findings.summary: The claim that a type switch compiles to a hash jump table is wrong — gc lowers type switches to a binary search over `typeHash` (with linear compares for few cases); jump tables are used for dense integer/string switches, not type switches.
findings.evidence: "A type switch compiles to a hash jump, not a linear scan"
findings.fix: Rewrite as "A large type switch compiles to a binary search over the type hash, not a linear scan".

findings.summary: The callout states interface comparison panics whenever the held type is a slice, map or func, omitting that it only panics when both operands have the *same* uncomparable dynamic type.
findings.evidence: "Comparison checks type and value. If the held type is a slice, map or func it panics at run time."
findings.fix: Say "If both sides hold the *same* uncomparable dynamic type (slice, map, func) it panics; differing dynamic types just compare false."

findings.summary: The blanket claim that an `interface{}` container allocates once per element contradicts the page's own list of allocation-free boxing cases.
findings.evidence: "An `interface{}` container costs one allocation per element" vs. "Free cases: pointers, cached small ints, devirtualized calls"
findings.fix: Qualify it: "An `interface{}` container costs one allocation per boxed non-pointer element".

findings.summary: The `Alloc` column for the generic row is wrong: GC-shape stenciling is a compile-time instantiation/dictionary concern, not a per-call allocation — generic code does not box its type parameter.
findings.evidence: table row ["generic","often yes","per GC shape"] under headers ["Call kind","Inlining","Alloc"]
findings.fix: Change the Alloc cell to "none" and, if the stenciling point matters, move "one instantiation per GC shape" into a bullet.

findings.summary: Gotcha #4 (range-variable capture) is stated only as a table cell and a one-line bullet with no code, making it the one gotcha in the list a learner cannot picture.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["4","`&v` of a range variable","Go 1.22, or copy"] plus the bullet "Pre-1.22 every `&v` in a range aliases one variable" — no loop is ever shown in Part 2.
findings.fix: Add the two-line snippet from the syllabus next to the table: `for _, v := range items { list = append(list, &v) }` with the comment that pre-1.22 every element of `list` points at the same variable, and the fix `v := v` (or Go 1.22+).

findings.summary: The second fix offered for the `String()` recursion is asserted with no example, unlike the bug itself which is shown in code.
findings.evidence: "Or convert to a method-less local type first" follows the code block `return fmt.Sprintf("%v", p) // infinite!` but no conversion is shown.
findings.fix: Show the idiom in the same code block: `type plain P` then `return fmt.Sprintf("%v", plain(p))`, with a note that the local type drops the method set and stops the recursion.
